title: Ecma International TC39-relevant MDN issues
description: Issue filed on MDN Web Docs related to pages attached to technologies developed by Ecma International TC39

items.content_html:
MDN URL

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Statements/try...catch

What specific section or headline is this issue about?

The finally block

What information was incorrect, unhelpful, or incomplete?

The third bullet point states: “Immediately before the execution of a control-flow statement (return, throw, break, continue) in the try block or catch block that would exit the block.” However, if control flow reaches a return statement in the try block, that statement is still executed (including any side effects it may produce). The finally block runs afterward, but it does not prevent the return statement itself from being evaluated. Only if the finally block contains its own return statement does it override the previous one, causing the function to return the value associated with the return statement in finally.

What did you expect to see?

The finally block

The finally block contains statements to execute after the try block and catch block(s) execute, but before the statements following the try...catch...finally block. Control flow will always enter the finally block, which can proceed in one of the following ways:

  • Immediately after the control flow exits the try block in a try...finally construct (e.g., after the last statement or a throw or return statement);
  • Immediately after the control flow exits the catch block in a try...catch...finally construct;
  • Immediately after the control flow exits the try block in a try...catch...finally construct, unless it exits via a throw statement (in which case control flow enters the catch block first);

The following example shows one use case for the finally block. The code opens a file and then executes statements that use the file; the finally block makes sure the file always closes after it is used even if an exception was thrown.

openMyFile();
try {
  // tie up a resource
  writeMyFile(theData);
} finally {
  closeMyFile(); // always close the resource
}

If control flow reaches a return statement in the try block and no return statement is present in the finally block, all statements in the finally block are still executed before the function returns the value associated with this statement.

function doIt() {
  try {
    return 1; // evaluated first
  } finally {
    console.log("enter finally"); // executed after
    // the function now returns 1
  }
}
doIt(); // returns 1

It is generally a bad idea to use control flow statements (return, throw, break, continue) in the finally block. The finally block always runs after the try and catch blocks, even if they exit because of a control flow statement. If finally itself contains a control flow statement, it takes precedence over the one from try or catch. This means it can change a returned value or replace a thrown exception. For this reason, the finally block should generally be reserved for cleanup code.

The following examples illustrate how this happens in practice.

If control flow reaches two return statements (possibly in the try and finally blocks or in the catch and finally blocks), both statements are evaluated in the correct order (which matters in the case of side effects). Only the function's returned value will be the one associated with the last return statement evaluated (which is the one in the finally block).

function doIt() {
  let order = '';
  try {
    return order = order + 'return try, ';
  } finally {
    return order = order + 'return finally.';
  }
}
doIt(); // returns 'return try, return finally.'

The same applies to other control flow statements (throw, break, continue).

function doIt() {
  try {
    throw 'try'; // makes control flow enter the `catch` block
  } catch {
    throw 'catch'; // makes control flow enter the `finally` block
  } finally {
    throw 'finally'; // changes the thrown value from 'catch' to 'finally'
  }
}
doIt(); // throws 'finally'

No response

items.content_html:
MDN URL

https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Practical_implementation_guides/CORP

What specific section or headline is this issue about?

Examples

What information was incorrect, unhelpful, or incomplete?

I believe SharedArrayBuffer is enabled by COOP + COEP, not CORP and CORP only affects resources, not the enabling of SharedArrayBuffer itself.

Affected text:

Instruct browsers to allow cross-origin resource access, including access to features with unthrottled timers (such as SharedArrayBuffer objects or Performance.now()):

Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp

This also permits such resources to be embedded.

What did you expect to see?

To enable SharedArrayBuffer and performance.now(), the document must be cross-origin isolated environment. Include the following headers on the document:

Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp

A page using Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp may only load resources that explicitly allow being embedded.
Resources can opt in using either:

Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy (CORP):

Cross-Origin-Resource-Policy: cross-origin

or CORS:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://example.com

CORP and CORS do not themselves enable SharedArrayBuffer they only allow resources to be loaded under COEP so that isolation is maintained.

Do you have any supporting links, references, or citations?

No response

Do you have anything more you want to share?

Please suggest if there any improvements are needed to the proposed text, if everything looks good, I would be happy to open a pull to update the documentation.
items.title: [hr-time-3, ecmascript] Fix: CORP does not enable SharedArrayBuffer
